title: Credit-decay and burst decomposition — PRD (draft)
body:
Summary

This is an early PRD sketch for a complementary approach to dedicated-capacity burst handling that focuses on two levers: a time-decayed credit ledger for tenant burst budgets, and a burst decomposition agent that attempts to split large requests into smaller atomic operations where feasible. The overall goal is to improve perceived latency for latency-sensitive tenants while preserving fairness and avoiding expensive hard preemption.

Why this problem matters

Existing dedicated strategies concentrate on static pockets of reserved capacity plus ad-hoc burst credits. We observe two common customer pain points:
- Spikes from batch-heavy tenants exhaust shared headroom and either push other tenants into hard throttling or trigger expensive provisioning.
- A small number of high-cost requests (long-context or high-temperature sampling) create tail latency spikes for colocated tenants.

High-level proposal

1) Credit-decay ledger: per-tenant credit accounts are accrued by steady usage and decay over a configurable half-life. Credits are consumed by burst requests; when credits are low, the system applies progressively stronger soft-degradation policies (prefetch hints, smaller max tokens, optional sampling adjustments) before resorting to rejection.

2) Burst decomposition agent: a runtime layer that can transform a single large request into an orchestrated set of sub-requests (microbursts) with local KV cache hints and result-merging logic. Decomposition is best-effort and controlled by tenant policy; for some models and prompts it will not be applicable.

3) Soft-isolation envelopes: dynamically sized latency envelopes per tenant. When other tenants are starved of headroom, the system applies temporary narrowing of envelope for low-priority tenants, backed by a priority-weighted queue. The envelope restricts max concurrent requests and an admission time budget.

Key design details

Credit-decay model
- Each tenant t has a credit balance C_t. Credits are earned at a baseline rate R_base for steady-state reserved capacity usage and optionally boosted for off-peak hours.
- Credits decay with continuous half-life H (configurable per pool). Decay formula: C_t(t_now) = C_t(t_last) * 2^{-(delta / H)}.
- Burst cost: a burst request consumes credits proportional to estimated token cost plus an overhead factor for high memory or long-latency kernels.
- Grace tiers: >X credits => immediate admit, >Y credits => admit with soft-degradation (sampling/temp reduce tokens), <=Y credits => queue or reject depending on SLA.

Burst decomposition agent
- Decomposition is a policy-based transformer component sitting before admission control. Policies include: split-by-turn, split-by-prompt-chunk, staged-generation with shorter context warmups.
- The agent annotates sub-requests with reuse keys for KV cache locality. Example flow: large-doc-summarize => split into N sections, run summary per section, merge via short-coh summary step.
- Fallback semantics: if decomposition fails or quality loss is unacceptable, the original request may be admitted consuming full cost or deferred. Tenants can opt-out.

Soft-isolation envelopes and priority-weighted queueing
- Envelope parameters: max-concurrency, admission-timeout, min-allowed-credits. Envelopes adjust automatically based on pool utilization percentiles.
- Priority weights map to a token-cost-to-service multiplier; higher weight reduces admitted microbursts during contention.

Operator and API surface
- API additions (backwards compatible): request metadata fields: tenant_hint, decomposition_policy: [auto|off|heuristic], credit_billing_override (enterprise only).
- Console surfaces: per-tenant credit timeline chart, envelope heatmap, decomposition success/failure rate.
- Admin: controls to tune half-life H, baseline accrual rate R_base per pool, and envelope aggressiveness.

Metrics and SLOs
- Primary metrics: 95/99 token latency per pool, per-tenant admitted burst ratio, decomposition-success-rate, credit-burn-rate, soft-degrade-rate.
- SLO targets: keep 95th latency for premium tenants within 1.2x baseline under up to 3x steady traffic bursts; aim to keep soft-degrade incidents <5% for premium.

Simulation plan (must ship before wide rollout)
- Build a simulator that replays production traces and supports the following knobs: H, R_base, burst-cost-mapping, decomposition-hit-rate, envelope-sensitivity.
- Run grid search across realistic traces (week-of-monthly spike, Black Friday analog) and measure fairness (Gini of admitted throughput), cost (extra GPU-minutes), and latency tail improvements.
- Target sample experiments: 100 tenants mixed small/medium/large; 10% produce repeated microbursts, 5% produce 1 large batch every 10 minutes.

Experiments and acceptance criteria
- Experiment A: Credit-only (no decomposition) vs baseline. Acceptance: reduce hard rejections by >30% and not increase cost by >10%.
- Experiment B: Add decomposition with heuristics. Acceptance: decomposition success >70% on eligible requests and 95th latency improvement for small tenants >15%.
- Experiment C: Full stack with envelopes. Acceptance: premium tenant 99th latency within SLA 95% of time during simulated 5x spikes.

Rollout and operator runbook (brief)
- Stage 0: internal-only canary on non-prod pools, run simulator-driven smoke tests.
- Stage 1: opt-in tenant beta (select mid-market customers) with decomposition opt-out. Monitor credit burn and user-reported quality regression.
- Stage 2: auto-enroll with conservative half-life. Increase aggressiveness only after 2 weeks of stable metrics.

Risks and mitigations
- Quality regression from decomposition: require human-in-the-loop sampling and a metric for semantic drift. Provide per-tenant quality rollback knob.
- Complexity operations burden: initial flagging to limit to a single pool operator team; build visualization and alerts for unusual credit drains.
- Gaming credits: enforce policy that prevents trivial work to earn credits (e.g., limit accrual rate to useful tokens only).

Open questions (short list)
- How to accurately estimate burst cost pre-admission for highly variable prompts?
- Should enterprise tenants be allowed to purchase permanent credit multipliers? (pricing implications)
- How to surface decomposition transparency to end-users without exposing internal heuristics?

Immediate next steps (owner: Priya)
- Prototype credit decay simulator and run against week-of-production trace (owner: Linh). Due: 2 weeks.
- Small patch on API to accept decomposition_policy metadata and record telemetry (owner: Marcus). Due: 1 week.
- Design console mock for credit timeline and envelope heatmap (owner: Evan). Due: 2 weeks.

Appendix: pseudo admission logic (informal)
- On request arrival: estimate_cost = cheap_estimator(request); if decomposition_policy != off and estimator predicts benefit => attempt decomposition; if decomposed => enqueue sub-requests with reuse keys; else continue.
- Ledger check: if C_t > immediate_threshold => admit; else if C_t > soft_threshold => admit_with_soft_degrade; else enqueue_or_reject_based_on_priority().

Notes and references
- See linked Confluence doc for experiment traces and earlier sketches. This doc intentionally focuses on the product surface and simulation acceptance criteria.

Notes to self: keep decomposition opt-out obvious in tenant settings. Plan a frontend banner during beta that explains possible changes in output shape when decomposition is active.
